questions.question: What does object detection tell you that image classification does not?
questions.answer: Where the objects are (their bounding boxes), not only which objects are present.
questions.explanation: The opening paragraph says detection lets you know which objects are in a picture and where they are.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the applications listed on the page?
options: Counting
Tracking
Cropping
Denoising
questions.answer: Denoising
questions.explanation: The page lists counting, tracking and cropping. Denoising is an image-restoration task, not mentioned.

questions.question: How is tracking implemented according to the page?
questions.answer: By running object detection on every frame of a video and following how the detected objects move.
questions.explanation: The tracking bullet describes per-frame detection.

questions.question: Why would you crop a detected object and send a higher-resolution patch to a classifier or OCR model?
questions.answer: The detector can work on a downscaled whole image, while the specialised model gets the fine detail it needs only for the relevant region.
questions.explanation: The cropping bullet describes this pipeline; the efficiency reasoning is an explanation beyond the page's wording.

questions.question: Can you name the two families of detectors the chapter will compare, and which kind you will train from scratch?
questions.answer: Two-stage and single-stage detectors; a simple single-stage detector (YOLO) is trained from scratch.
questions.explanation: From the 'This chapter covers' list and the chapter outline (12.1, 12.2).

questions.question: According to the page, why would you choose object detection over segmentation?
options: Detection gives more information than segmentation
Detection is faster to run and its training labels are much cheaper to produce
Segmentation cannot handle multiple objects
Segmentation models cannot be trained on photographs
questions.answer: Detection is faster to run and its training labels are much cheaper to produce
questions.explanation: The page names a computational cost and a data labeling cost. Detection gives less information, not more; segmentation handles multiple objects fine; and nothing restricts segmentation to non-photographs.

questions.question: Explain what it means that segmentation is a 'strict superset' of detection.
questions.answer: Every detection output (a box) can be computed from an instance mask by taking its smallest enclosing rectangle, but a mask cannot be recovered from a box, so segmentation carries all of detection's information plus more.
questions.explanation: This is the argument of the first two paragraphs: box from mask is possible, mask from box is not.

questions.question: Name the two broad families of object detection architectures and give one example model of each.
questions.answer: Two-stage detectors (R-CNN models) and single-stage detectors (RetinaNet or YOLO).
questions.explanation: Listed in the two bullets of section 12.1.

questions.question: What does the first stage of an R-CNN produce?
options: A single refined box per object
A per-pixel segmentation mask
A few thousand partially overlapping bounding boxes around object-like areas
A class probability for the whole image
questions.answer: A few thousand partially overlapping bounding boxes around object-like areas
questions.explanation: Stated at the bottom of the page (continuing on p.355). Refined single boxes come at the end of the pipeline; masks belong to segmentation; whole-image probabilities are classification.

questions.question: Give an application where you would use detection and one where you would need segmentation, justifying each with the page's criterion.
questions.answer: Counting objects only needs locations, so detection suffices; measuring an object's exact outline or area needs pixel-level information, so segmentation is required.
questions.explanation: The page's rule: use detection if you have no need for pixel-level information, e.g. counting.

questions.question: In figure 12.1, which classes are detected, and what does the layout of the boxes show about detector output?
questions.answer: Person, horse and tie; boxes overlap and nest (riders' boxes lie within horses' boxes), showing each detection is an independent labelled rectangle.
questions.explanation: Read from the figure; unlike semantic segmentation, a pixel can lie inside several boxes.

questions.question: Can you sketch, from memory, the difference in pipeline between a two-stage and a single-stage detector?
questions.answer: Two-stage: image → region proposals → ConvNet classification per proposal → refined boxes. Single-stage: image → one network that predicts boxes and labels jointly.
questions.explanation: Check yourself against the mermaid diagram and p.355–356.

questions.question: What replaced Selective Search as the first stage in later R-CNN versions such as Faster R-CNN?
options: A Region Proposal Network
A segmentation model
A sliding-window SVM
Non-maximum suppression
questions.answer: A Region Proposal Network
questions.explanation: The page states the box generation stage became a deep learning model called a Region Proposal Network. A segmentation model is the authors' alternative to R-CNN, not a component; sliding-window SVMs and NMS are not mentioned as the proposal stage.

questions.question: How does the book define 'heuristic', and what two kinds of models is it contrasted with?
questions.answer: A bundle of hard-coded rules someone made up; contrasted with learned models (rules derived automatically) and theory-derived models.
questions.explanation: Quoted from the paragraph on Selective Search.

questions.question: List the steps stage 2 of an R-CNN performs after receiving the region proposals.
questions.answer: Classify each proposal into predetermined classes with a ConvNet; discard proposals with low scores across all classes; refine the remaining boxes to eliminate duplicates and make them precise.
questions.explanation: These three steps appear in the second paragraph.

questions.question: What is the main reason the page gives for R-CNN's computational expense?
options: It uses very high-resolution input images
It must classify thousands of patches for every image
It trains two separate datasets
It predicts a mask for every pixel
questions.answer: It must classify thousands of patches for every image
questions.explanation: Stated directly. Resolution and datasets are not mentioned; per-pixel masks describe segmentation.

questions.question: Summarize the authors' argument that you generally don't need R-CNN in practical applications.
questions.answer: If you have a beefy server GPU, a segmentation model like Segment Anything gives more information; if you're resource-constrained, a single-stage detector is more efficient. Either way, an expensive two-stage detector is not the best choice.
questions.explanation: This is the 'My take' passage closing the section.

questions.question: Why is it acceptable for R-CNN's first stage to be 'not very smart'?
questions.answer: Because the second stage classifies every proposal and discards low-scoring ones, so the first stage only needs to propose plenty of object-like areas, not decide what they are.
questions.explanation: Inference from the division of labour described in the first two paragraphs.

questions.question: Could you redraw figure 12.2 and annotate where filtering and duplicate elimination happen?
questions.answer: Input → Stage 1 (region proposals) → Stage 2 CNN (class scores) → discard low scores → refine/deduplicate → final boxes.
questions.explanation: Compare with the mermaid diagram above.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT named on the page as a family of single-stage detectors?
options: RetinaNet
SSD
YOLO
Faster R-CNN
questions.answer: Faster R-CNN
questions.explanation: Faster R-CNN is a two-stage detector (p.355). RetinaNet, SSD and YOLO are the single-stage families listed here.

questions.question: What trade-off do single-stage detectors make relative to two-stage detectors, according to the page?
questions.answer: Significantly faster speed and greater efficiency, with a minor potential tradeoff in accuracy.
questions.explanation: Quoted from the second paragraph of 12.1.2.

questions.question: Why do the authors choose to recreate the original 2015 YOLO instead of a recent version?
questions.answer: Because the original is simpler to work with, and building a detector already requires a lot of box-manipulation code; keeping the model simple keeps the chapter manageable.
questions.explanation: Stated in the opening paragraph of 12.2.

questions.question: Which COCO annotations does the chapter use?
options: Segmentation masks only
Bounding boxes (with object labels), not masks
Captions only
Both masks and boxes
questions.answer: Bounding boxes (with object labels), not masks
questions.explanation: The authors disregard the segmentation masks and use just bounding boxes; labels are also used (p.357). Captions aren't mentioned.

questions.question: In listing 12.1, what does `extract=True` do, and what does `images_path` hold?
questions.answer: It makes `get_file` unpack the downloaded zip; `images_path` holds the local path of the downloaded/extracted COCO images, later joined with `/train2017/` and a file name.
questions.explanation: See the code explanation; usage of `images_path` appears in listing 12.2 on p.357.

questions.question: How does COCO's inclusion of both masks and boxes relate to the argument on p.354?
questions.answer: It illustrates that segmentation annotations are a superset of detection annotations: the same dataset can train a segmenter, but the cheaper boxes are all a detector needs.
questions.explanation: An inference connecting the dataset description to the strict-superset argument.

questions.question: Can you explain to someone why YOLO is called a single-stage detector and why that makes it suitable for real-time video?
questions.answer: It predicts all boxes and labels in one pass of one network instead of classifying thousands of proposals, so it can keep up with incoming frames.
questions.explanation: Combines pp.355–356.

questions.question: Using `scale_box`, convert the box [40, 60, 120, 80] on a portrait image of width 300 and height 400.
questions.explanation: Height > width, so x is shifted by half of the width deficit; y is not shifted.

questions.question: What does `images = {image["id"]: image for image in annotations["images"]}` actually do?
options: Sorts the images by file name
Builds a dictionary mapping image IDs to image records
Loads every image from disk
Removes images without annotations
questions.answer: Builds a dictionary mapping image IDs to image records
questions.explanation: It is a dict comprehension keyed by ID, used for lookup in the loop. Nothing is sorted (despite the callout), no pixels are loaded, and no filtering happens on this line.

questions.question: What three keys does each element of `metadata` contain, and what is in each?
questions.answer: `boxes` — the list of normalized [x, y, w, h] boxes; `labels` — the list of COCO category IDs; `path` — the image file path under train2017/.
questions.explanation: See lines 19–24 of listing 12.2.

questions.question: Why does rescaling boxes to a unit square make later code simpler?
questions.answer: Boxes no longer depend on each image's pixel size, so they remain valid after images are resized to a common input size and can be manipulated (e.g. mapped to a grid) without consulting each image's dimensions.
questions.explanation: The page: 'This will make it easier to manipulate these boxes without needing to check the size of each input image.'

questions.question: Why does `scale_box` add an offset to y for a landscape image?
options: To convert the top-left corner into the box centre
Because the image is assumed centred in a square, leaving padding above and below
To flip the y axis upward
To compensate for JPEG compression
questions.answer: Because the image is assumed centred in a square, leaving padding above and below
questions.explanation: The offset equals half the width–height difference (scaled), the height of the top padding band. Centre conversion happens later (p.363); there is no axis flip; compression is irrelevant.

questions.question: Would an image in `train2017` that has no annotations appear in `metadata`? Why?
questions.answer: No. Records are created only while iterating over annotations, so an image with none is never added.
questions.explanation: Follows from the structure of the loop in listing 12.2.

questions.question: Can you write the inverse of `scale_box` to recover pixel coordinates?
questions.answer: Subtract the same centring offset, then multiply by max(width, height).
questions.explanation: See the illustrative `unscale_box` in the code notes.

questions.question: From listing 12.3, how many images does `metadata` contain, and what is the range of boxes per image?
questions.answer: 117,266 images, with 1 to 63 boxes each.
questions.explanation: Printed by `len(metadata)` and the min/max list comprehensions.

questions.question: What hues does `label_to_color` assign to the first three new labels it sees?
questions.answer: len(color_map) is 1, 2, 3 (gray occupies key 0), so hues are 0.618, 0.236 (1.236 mod 1) and 0.854 (1.854 mod 1).
questions.explanation: Apply h = (k·0.618) mod 1 with k = len(color_map).

questions.question: Why does the code vary only the hue in HSV space?
options: Because RGB cannot represent bright colours
To keep all colours equally bright and vivid while making them distinct
Because Matplotlib only accepts HSV
To encode the label ID numerically in the colour
questions.answer: To keep all colours equally bright and vivid while making them distinct
questions.explanation: The page: fixing saturation and brightness and updating only the hue produces bright new colours that stand out. RGB can represent them; Matplotlib accepts RGB (hence `hsv_to_rgb`); the colour doesn't encode the ID.

questions.question: What does `max(max(x["labels"]) for x in metadata) + 1` actually measure, and why might it differ from the number of classes?
questions.answer: The size of the integer range 0..max ID. If IDs are non-contiguous (as in COCO, 80 classes with IDs up to 90), the range is larger than the number of distinct classes.
questions.explanation: See the review flag; the expression counts slots, not distinct labels.

questions.question: In `metadata[435]`, which box spans the entire width of the unit square?
options: The cat box
The bench box
The bicycle box
None of them
questions.answer: The bicycle box
questions.explanation: Its box is [0.0, 0.12, 1.0, 0.75] — x = 0, w = 1.0. The cat box has w = 0.57 and the bench box w = 0.79.

questions.question: Which Matplotlib object does `draw_box` add, and with which arguments?
questions.answer: A `Rectangle` patch at `(x, y)` with width `w`, height `h`, `lw=2`, `ec=color`, `fc="none"`, added via `ax.add_patch`.
questions.explanation: From the last line of listing 12.4 on this page.

questions.question: Could you explain why stepping hues by 0.618 is better than stepping by 0.1 or 0.5?
questions.answer: 0.5 alternates between two hues; 0.1 repeats after 10 and gives neighbours similar colours; 0.618 never repeats and keeps successive colours far apart.
questions.explanation: See the 'deeper' note on the golden ratio.

questions.question: For a portrait image of width 300 and height 400, compute `wpad`, `hpad` and the `extent` used by `draw_image`.
questions.explanation: Height > width, so only wpad is nonzero; extent = [wpad, 1 − wpad, 1 − hpad, hpad].

questions.question: Why does `draw_image` set `ylim=(1, 0)`?
options: To flip the image upside down
So that (0, 0) is at the top left and y grows downward, like image and COCO coordinates
To crop the padding
Because Matplotlib requires decreasing limits for images
questions.answer: So that (0, 0) is at the top left and y grows downward, like image and COCO coordinates
questions.explanation: The callout says the image is drawn with (0, 0) at the top left. The image is not flipped (extent accounts for the inversion), nothing is cropped, and Matplotlib doesn't require decreasing limits.

questions.question: Why must `draw_image` use the same padding convention as `scale_box` on p.357?
questions.answer: Because the boxes were normalized assuming the image is centred in a square scaled by its longer side; drawing the image any other way (e.g. stretched) would make the normalized boxes misalign with the objects.
questions.explanation: The offsets are identical: (W−H)/(2W) = hpad for landscape images.

questions.question: Where is each label text placed relative to its box, and which argument controls this?
questions.answer: Just above the box's top-left corner; `va="bottom"` anchors the text's bottom edge at (x, y).
questions.explanation: With the inverted y axis, the text extends upward (toward smaller y) from the corner.

questions.question: What does figure 12.3 actually display?
options: YOLO predictions on a test image
Ground-truth COCO boxes for metadata[435]
Region proposals from Selective Search
A segmentation mask of the cat
questions.answer: Ground-truth COCO boxes for metadata[435]
questions.explanation: The snippet draws `sample["boxes"]` from the annotations. No model has been trained, and no proposals or masks are involved — despite the caption's wording.

questions.question: Explain why the cat's box is blue, the bench's yellow-green and the bicycle's pink in figure 12.3.
questions.answer: `label_to_color` assigns hues in the order labels are first seen: 17 (cat) gets 0.618 (blue), 15 (bench) 0.236 (yellow-green), 2 (bicycle) 0.854 (pink).
questions.explanation: Connects the golden-ratio rule of p.358 to the figure.

questions.question: Could you adapt `draw_image` to take a NumPy array instead of a file path?
questions.answer: Skip `plt.imread` when given an array (e.g. check `isinstance(image, str)`), then compute padding and extent the same way.
questions.explanation: The rest of the function only needs the array's height and width.

questions.question: Why do the authors shuffle `metadata` after filtering it?
options: Because the images are grouped by object type, which would be terrible for training
Because shuffling halves the data size
Because the ResNet backbone requires randomly ordered inputs to load its weights
Because shuffling removes images with more than four boxes
questions.answer: Because the images are grouped by object type, which would be terrible for training
questions.explanation: The page states the images are grouped by object type. Halving the data comes from the filter, not the shuffle; the backbone's weights have nothing to do with data order; and the removal of crowded images is done by `filter`, not `shuffle`.

questions.question: What distinguishes YOLO, a single-stage detector, from a two-stage detector such as R-CNN?
questions.answer: A two-stage detector first identifies candidate object regions and then classifies them; YOLO proposes bounding boxes and labels in one go, in a single pass of one network.
questions.explanation: This is the definition given at the start of 12.2.2, contrasting with section 12.1.1.

questions.question: What is the role of the confidence score output with each box, and what value should it take in most grid cells?
questions.answer: It indicates whether an object is actually detected at that grid location: high when there is an object, zero when there is not. Since most cells contain no object, most confidences should be near zero.
questions.explanation: Because every cell always outputs a box, the confidence score is needed to separate real detections from empty cells.

questions.question: According to the page, why does the book switch from an Xception backbone to ResNet for object detection?
options: ResNet uses strides rather than pooling to downsample, and strided convolutions are better when spatial location matters
ResNet has no convolutional layers, so it is faster
Xception cannot be loaded from KerasHub
ResNet was the backbone used in the original YOLO paper
questions.answer: ResNet uses strides rather than pooling to downsample, and strided convolutions are better when spatial location matters
questions.explanation: The page gives exactly this reason, citing chapter 11. ResNet is convolutional; Xception has been loaded from KerasHub earlier in the book; and the YOLO authors created their own backbone rather than using ResNet.

questions.question: The book predicts only one box per grid cell. What kind of situation can such a model not handle, and how does the dataset filter on this page help?
questions.answer: Two objects whose centers fall in the same grid cell cannot both be predicted. Restricting training to images with at most four boxes makes such collisions rarer and the problem easier.
questions.explanation: The page states the simplification (one box per cell vs. multiple in the paper) and that filtering makes the problem easier; the link between the two is an inference.

questions.question: What input resolution does the book use, and what does it say about this choice?
questions.answer: Images are resized to 448 x 448; the book says image input size is quite important for the object detection task.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last paragraph of the page; listing 12.5 (p.361) sets `image_size = 448`.

questions.question: Without looking, sketch the output of the book's YOLO model for a single grid cell. Which quantities does it contain, and which one tells you whether to draw the box?
questions.answer: A bounding box, a confidence score and a class label; the confidence score decides whether the box is drawn.
questions.explanation: If you could list the three outputs and the role of confidence, you have the blueprint for listings 12.6 and 12.7.

questions.question: In the book's YOLO head, how are the numbers predicted for each grid location divided?
options: 5 for the box (4 coordinates + 1 confidence), the rest (91) for class predictions
4 for the box, 91 for classes, and the confidence is computed afterwards
91 for the box and 5 for the class
1 confidence per image and 4 coordinates per cell
questions.answer: 5 for the box (4 coordinates + 1 confidence), the rest (91) for class predictions
questions.explanation: The page states the first five numbers are for bounding box prediction (four for the box, one for confidence) and the rest form the class probability map over 91 labels. Confidence is predicted, not computed afterwards; the 91 values are class scores, not box values; and there is one confidence per cell, not per image.

questions.question: Why do `Backbone.from_preset` and `ImageConverter.from_preset` in listing 12.5 use the same preset string?
questions.answer: The converter supplies the preprocessing (resizing and rescaling) matching the pretrained backbone; loading it from the same preset ensures images are prepared exactly as the backbone expects.
questions.explanation: The book describes it as 'matching preprocessing (to rescale the image)' on p.360.

questions.question: In figure 12.4, what are the two intermediate outputs, and how are they combined into the final detections?
questions.answer: Bounding boxes with confidence scores and a class probability map. Confident boxes are kept and labeled with the class predicted for their grid cell, giving the final colored boxes for the person and the dog.
questions.explanation: The figure's middle panels are labeled 'Bounding boxes + confidence' and 'Class probability map' and both feed 'Final detections'.

questions.question: For a 6 x 6 grid with the output split described on this page, how many units must the final dense layer have?
questions.explanation: Each cell needs 96 numbers; listing 12.6's summary (p.362) shows `dense_7` with output shape `(None, 3456)`.

questions.question: Which description of the YOLO head recipe matches the page?
options: Feed the backbone output through two densely connected layers with an activation in the middle, then split the output
Feed each grid cell's crop through a separate classifier
Use a region-proposal network followed by RoI pooling
Apply a single softmax to the whole output, including the box coordinates
questions.answer: Feed the backbone output through two densely connected layers with an activation in the middle, then split the output
questions.explanation: That is the setup described in the text. Per-crop classifiers and region proposals belong to two-stage detectors; the softmax is applied only to the class part (p.362), never to box coordinates.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, what a KerasHub `Backbone` is and what it lacks compared with a full image classifier?
questions.answer: It is the pretrained convolutional feature extractor; it lacks the classification head (pooling and dense softmax layers), so it outputs feature maps instead of class probabilities.
questions.explanation: This is why the book can attach its own YOLO head on top.

questions.question: Verify the parameter count of `dense_6` in the summary.
questions.explanation: The input size is the flattened 6 x 6 x 512 feature map; each unit has one weight per input plus a bias.

questions.question: What is the output shape of the `Reshape` layer in listing 12.6?
questions.explanation: It reshapes the 3,456 outputs to `(grid_size, grid_size, num_labels + 5)`. `(6, 6, 91)` is the class slice after it, `(14, 14, ...)` is the backbone's spatial size, and `(None, 3456)` is the Dense output before reshaping.

questions.question: Why does only `x[..., 5:]` pass through a softmax?
questions.answer: Those 91 channels are class scores that must form a probability distribution per cell; the first five channels are box coordinates and confidence, which are not mutually exclusive categories and need different treatment.
questions.explanation: The code splits the predictions and applies the softmax only to the class part; the book notes the box outputs need special consideration later.

questions.question: Using the valid-convolution formula, show why `Conv2D(512, (3, 3), strides=(2, 2))` turns a 14 x 14 input into 6 x 6, and compute its parameter count.
questions.explanation: Conv2D defaults to 'valid' padding. The parameter count matches the summary row for `conv2d_3`.

questions.question: Why does listing 12.6 return `{"box": ..., "class": ...}` rather than a single tensor?
options: So that each output can be paired with its own target and loss during training
Because Keras models cannot output tensors with more than three dimensions
Because the backbone requires dictionary outputs
To make the model run faster at inference
questions.answer: So that each output can be paired with its own target and loss during training
questions.explanation: Multi-output models let Keras apply one loss per named output and sum them (p.366). Keras handles 4-D outputs fine, the backbone's interface is unrelated, and the dict has no speed effect.

questions.question: What would go wrong if you removed the strided `Conv2D` and flattened the backbone output directly into `Dense(2048)`?
questions.answer: The flattened vector would have 14 x 14 x 2048 = 401,408 values, so the dense layer would need roughly 822 million weights: far too many for memory and for the amount of training data.
questions.explanation: The book says 401,408 floats are 'a bit too many to feed into our dense layers' (p.363); the parameter count is simple arithmetic.

questions.question: Cover the summary table and write down the output shape of each layer of listing 12.6. Then compare with the printed summary.
questions.explanation: If you got all shapes, you understand how each layer transforms the tensor.

questions.question: Apply `to_grid` with `grid_size = 6` to the box `[0.0, 0.15, 0.79, 0.69]` (the bench box from p.358).
questions.explanation: cx = (0 + 0.395) x 6 = 2.37, cy = (0.15 + 0.345) x 6 = 2.97; int gives 2 and 2; offsets are the fractional parts; w and h are unchanged.

questions.question: In the book's YOLO encoding, what are `w` and `h` relative to?
options: The size of the whole image
The size of the responsible grid cell
The size of the backbone feature map in pixels
The size of the largest box in the image
questions.answer: The size of the whole image
questions.explanation: The page states that `w` and `h` represent the object's size relative to the image size; only `x` and `y` are relative to the grid cell. The feature map and other boxes play no role in the encoding.

questions.question: Why does the model downscale the backbone feature maps with a strided conv before the dense layers?
questions.answer: The backbone output (14, 14, 2048) is 401,408 floats per image, too many to feed into dense layers; the strided conv reduces it to (6, 6, 512), 18,432 floats.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph after the summary; the size of the flattened vector determines the first dense layer's parameter count.

questions.question: The book says there is 'no locality constraint' in the head and that this is by design. Explain what this means and why it is desirable here.
questions.answer: Because the entire feature map is flattened into dense layers, each grid cell's predictions depend on features from the whole image. This is desirable because large objects extend beyond a single cell, and the cell responsible for an object's center must be able to see its full extent to predict w and h.
questions.explanation: Direct paraphrase of the last paragraph before section 12.2.3, with the w/h reasoning as an elaboration.

questions.question: Which grid cell is responsible for predicting a given ground-truth box?
options: The cell in which the box's center falls
The cell containing the box's top-left corner
Every cell the box overlaps
The cell with the highest predicted confidence
questions.answer: The cell in which the box's center falls
questions.explanation: 'Each grid detector will be responsible for detecting any boxes whose center falls inside the grid box.' The top-left corner is the dataset's storage format, overlap is used only for the class map (p.364), and the assignment is fixed by the data, not by predictions.

questions.question: What do the 53,248 non-trainable parameters in the summary tell you about how the backbone is used?
questions.answer: Almost all parameters (77,797,088) are trainable, so the backbone is fine-tuned along with the head rather than frozen; the small non-trainable remainder is model state such as (most likely) batch-normalization statistics.
questions.explanation: The trainable/non-trainable split is printed on the page; attributing the remainder to batch-norm statistics is an inference.

questions.question: Without looking at the code, write `to_grid` yourself and then derive `from_grid` as its inverse. Check your version against p.363-364.
questions.answer: to_grid: center = (x + w/2, y + h/2) x S; index = int(center); offset = center - index. from_grid: x = (xi + dx)/S - w/2, y = (yi + dy)/S - h/2.
questions.explanation: Being able to derive the inverse confirms you understand the encoding.

questions.question: What does `box_array[index, yi, xi] = [*grid_box, 1.0]` store?
options: The cell-relative center offsets, the image-relative width and height, and a confidence of 1
The top-left corner and size of the box in image coordinates, and the label
The class probabilities of the box
The box coordinates for every cell the box intersects
questions.answer: The cell-relative center offsets, the image-relative width and height, and a confidence of 1
questions.explanation: `grid_box` comes from `to_grid` (offsets dx, dy plus w, h) and 1.0 is the confidence. It is not in image coordinates, contains no label or probabilities, and is written only at the center cell.

questions.question: For a box `[0.5, 0.0, 0.2, 0.3]` with `grid_size = 6`, which cells does the first loop of listing 12.7 label, and which cell gets the box target?
questions.answer: Columns floor(3.0) = 3 to ceil(4.2) = 5 (exclusive), i.e. 3-4; rows floor(0) = 0 to ceil(1.8) = 2, i.e. 0-1: four cells. Center (0.6, 0.15) gives cx = 3.6, cy = 0.9, so the box target goes to cell (xi, yi) = (3, 0) with offsets (0.6, 0.9).
questions.explanation: Apply the floor/ceil bounds for the class map and `to_grid` for the box target.

questions.question: What confidence values do the box targets contain, and why are the zeros important?
questions.answer: 1.0 in each cell holding a real box center, 0 everywhere else. The zeros teach the model to output near-zero confidence in the many cells that contain no object.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second bullet; it connects to the goal stated on p.360 that most grid locations report near-zero confidence.

questions.question: Why does listing 12.7 use two separate loops instead of writing the class block and the center box in one loop?
questions.answer: With one loop, a box processed later could overwrite, in its class block, the center cell of an earlier box, leaving that box's center with the wrong label. Doing all class blocks first and then the centers (with `class_array[index, yi, xi] = label`) ensures the label at each center matches its box.
questions.explanation: The callout 'Makes sure the class label for the box's center location matches the box' describes this purpose.

questions.question: Which limitation of these targets does the text explicitly acknowledge?
options: Overlapping boxes are not handled
Boxes larger than one cell cannot be represented
Only one image can be processed at a time
Confidence values are not stored
questions.answer: Overlapping boxes are not handled
questions.explanation: 'To keep our code simple, we won't worry about overlapping boxes.' Large boxes are represented via image-relative w, h; all images are processed; confidence is stored as the fifth value.

questions.question: What value marks a grid cell with no object in `class_array`, and why does that work for COCO?
questions.answer: 0, from `np.zeros`. COCO category ids start at 1, so 0 is free to mean 'no object' (and the drawing code maps 0 to no color/gray).
questions.explanation: The array is zero-initialized and only cells under boxes are overwritten with real labels.

questions.question: Pick a box from `metadata[435]` (p.358) and compute by hand both its class-map cell range and its box target. Did you index the array as [row, column]?
questions.answer: For example the cat box: rows 1-3, columns 0-4 labeled 17; `box_array[i, 2, 2] = [0.43, 0.61, 0.57, 0.33, 1.0]`.
questions.explanation: Row = y index, column = x index; mixing them up is the most common bug with this encoding.

questions.question: In `draw_prediction(..., cutoff=1.0)` applied to the targets, which boxes are drawn?
options: Only boxes in cells holding a real box center (confidence 1.0)
All 36 boxes, one per grid cell
Every cell whose class label is non-zero
No boxes, because confidences are never above 1.0
questions.answer: Only boxes in cells holding a real box center (confidence 1.0)
questions.explanation: The condition is `confidence >= cutoff`; targets have confidence 1.0 only at box centers. All 36 would be drawn only with no cutoff; labeled cells are tinted but not drawn as boxes; `>=` includes 1.0.

questions.question: Using `draw_prediction`'s formula, what rectangle is drawn for grid cell (xi, yi) = (4, 2) with `grid_size = 6`?
questions.explanation: `x, y, w, h = (v / grid_size for v in (xi, yi, 1.0, 1.0))`.

questions.question: Where does the label of each drawn box come from, given that the box array has no label channel?
questions.answer: From the class map at the box's own grid cell: `label = classes[yi, xi]`.
questions.explanation: Listing 12.7 ensured the class label at each center cell matches the box; listing 12.8 relies on that.

questions.question: Why does figure 12.5 have white bands above and below the photo, and what does that imply for the top and bottom rows of the grid?
questions.answer: The photo is wider than tall, so `draw_image` pads it vertically to fit the unit square (as `scale_box` did for the boxes). The top and bottom grid rows therefore lie mostly over padding, where no object centers can fall.
questions.explanation: Padding logic is in `draw_image` (p.359) and `scale_box` (p.357); the consequence for grid rows is an inference.

questions.question: Why does the caption use `max(confidence, 0)`?
options: To avoid displaying negative confidence values, which a linear box output can produce
To convert confidence to a percentage
To select the most confident box in the image
To round confidence to two decimal places
questions.answer: To avoid displaying negative confidence values, which a linear box output can produce
questions.explanation: The box slice of the model has no activation (p.362), so predicted confidences can be negative; clamping keeps the display sensible. Percentage conversion and rounding are done by nothing / by `:.2f` respectively, and `max(..., 0)` compares with 0, not across boxes.

questions.question: What would `draw_prediction(path, box_array[0], class_array[0])` (no cutoff) draw, and why might that be useful?
questions.answer: It would attempt to draw all 36 boxes: the real ones plus, for every empty cell, a degenerate zero-width, zero-height box at the cell's top-left corner (decoded from an all-zero vector), captioned with its cell's class name and confidence 0.00. (Whether `coco_id_to_name` accepts label 0 is not shown in the book.) It is useful for inspecting raw model predictions, where you want to see every box regardless of confidence.
questions.explanation: `if not cutoff` is True for `None`, so the condition passes for every cell.

questions.question: Look at figure 12.5 and identify (a) the cells labeled with the giraffe class, (b) the responsible cell for the giraffe box, and (c) what the '1.00' means.
questions.answer: (a) The tinted block of cells under the giraffe's box; (b) the cell containing the giraffe box's center, from which the single box is drawn; (c) the target confidence for a real box, always 1.
questions.explanation: If you can map each visual element to `class_array`, `box_array` and the confidence channel, you understand the target encoding.

questions.question: In Listing 12.9, what does `dataset.take(500)` return?
options: The first 500 images
The first 500 batches of 16 image-label pairs
500 randomly chosen images
The first 500 file paths
questions.answer: The first 500 batches of 16 image-label pairs
questions.explanation: take is called on the dataset after .batch(16), so each element is a batch. It is not random (take preserves order; randomness comes from the earlier shuffle of metadata), and the elements are processed images with labels, not paths.

questions.question: Why does the label dataset use the keys 'box' and 'class'?
questions.answer: They match the names of the model's two outputs, so Keras pairs each target with the right output and its loss.
questions.explanation: The model in Listing 12.6 returns {'box': box_predictions, 'class': class_predictions}, and compile uses a loss dict with the same keys (p.368).

questions.question: Explain in your own words what prefetch(2) does and why it speeds training.
questions.answer: It keeps two batches prepared in a buffer while the model trains on the current one, overlapping CPU loading/resizing with accelerator computation so training doesn't pause each step.
questions.explanation: The NOTE states prefetch(2) keeps two batches buffered so training isn't interrupted to load and resize more images.

questions.question: Using the basic YOLO box loss, compute the localization error for an occupied cell with target (x, y, w, h) = (0.3, 0.7, 0.4, 0.2) and prediction (0.5, 0.6, 0.4, 0.1). What is the contribution of an empty cell that predicts (0.9, 0.9, 0.5, 0.5)?
questions.answer: 0.04 + 0.01 + 0 + 0.01 = 0.06; the empty cell contributes 0 localization error.
questions.explanation: Sum-squared error over the four parameters; the error is only computed for cells with actual boxes, so the empty cell is masked out.

questions.question: Which loss does the book use for the class output of the YOLO model?
options: mean_squared_error
binary_crossentropy
sparse_categorical_crossentropy
A custom IoU loss
questions.answer: sparse_categorical_crossentropy
questions.explanation: The class map holds integer labels per cell and the model outputs a softmax over 91 classes, so sparse categorical crossentropy fits. MSE and the IoU-based loss belong to the box output; binary crossentropy is for single-probability outputs.

questions.question: Why is the box confidence the 'tricky part' of the loss?
questions.answer: Because it should express how good the predicted box is, not just whether an object exists; that target depends on the current prediction (via IoU), so it can't be a fixed label and needs a custom loss.
questions.explanation: The page says the authors wanted confidence to reflect box quality; p.367 makes the IoU of predicted and true box the target.

questions.question: Could you rewrite Listing 12.9 so that the validation split holds exactly 500 images and the training data is reshuffled each epoch?
questions.answer: Split the zipped, unbatched dataset with take(500)/skip(500), then apply shuffle(...) and batch(16).prefetch(2) to the training part and batch(16) to the validation part.
questions.explanation: Order of operations determines whether take counts images or batches; shuffle must come before batch to mix individual samples.

questions.question: Compute the IoU of boxes (cx, cy, w, h) = (0.4, 0.4, 0.2, 0.2) and (0.5, 0.5, 0.2, 0.2).
questions.explanation: Box 1 spans [0.3, 0.5] in both axes, box 2 spans [0.4, 0.6]; the overlap is [0.4, 0.5] in each axis.

questions.question: What is the target confidence for a grid cell that contains an object?
options: Always 1
The IoU between the current predicted box and the actual box
The class probability of the object
questions.answer: The IoU between the current predicted box and the actual box
questions.explanation: The page says the IoU score between the current prediction and the actual box is used. 1 is what box_array stores but not the loss target; class probabilities belong to the class output; 0.5 is the weight for empty cells, not a target.

questions.question: Why does intersection_over_union use ops.divide_no_nan rather than a plain division?
questions.answer: If both boxes have zero area (e.g. clamped negative sizes), the union is 0; divide_no_nan returns 0 instead of NaN, keeping the loss and gradients finite.
questions.explanation: Areas are clamped with ops.maximum(..., 0.0), so zero unions can really occur during early training.

questions.question: Why does YOLO scale down the confidence loss in empty cells?
questions.answer: Most grid cells are empty, so their zero-confidence errors would dominate the total loss and drown out the signal from the few cells containing objects.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second bullet; with a 6 x 6 grid and at most four boxes, at least 32 of 36 cells are empty.

questions.question: What is the purpose of taking the square root of width and height before computing the loss?
options: To ensure widths are positive
To stop large boxes from mattering disproportionately more than small boxes
To speed up computation
To convert widths to grid units
questions.answer: To stop large boxes from mattering disproportionately more than small boxes
questions.explanation: That is the reason given in the third bullet. The sign-preserving version explicitly allows negative widths, so it doesn't ensure positivity; it does not speed anything up or change units.

questions.question: Using square roots, compare the width error when a target width of 0.04 is predicted as 0.09 with the error when a target width of 0.64 is predicted as 0.69.
questions.answer: Small box: (0.2 - 0.3)^2 = 0.01. Large box: (0.8 - 0.8307)^2 ≈ 0.00094. The same 0.05 absolute error costs about 10x more on the small box.
questions.explanation: sqrt compresses large values, so equal absolute errors weigh more for small boxes, as the third bullet intends.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why the confidence target must be computed inside the loss instead of being stored in the dataset?
questions.answer: Because it is the IoU of the model's current prediction with the true box, which changes at every training step.
questions.explanation: If you can state this, you understand why the page says 'This calls for a custom loss function.'

questions.question: In box_loss, what weight does the confidence error receive in a cell that contains an object?
questions.explanation: ops.where(no_object, conf_error * 0.5, conf_error) leaves it unscaled in occupied cells. 0.5 applies to empty cells, 5 to placement errors, and 0 is what placement errors get in empty cells.

questions.question: Why does the code slice conf_true as true[..., 4:] rather than true[..., 4]?
questions.answer: To keep a trailing axis of size 1 so the mask (B, 6, 6, 1) broadcasts against the (B, 6, 6, 2) errors and the confidence error can be concatenated with them.
questions.explanation: That is also why iou (B, 6, 6) needs ops.expand_dims(iou, -1).

questions.question: A cell has target (0.5, 0.5, 0.25, 0.36, 1) and prediction (0.4, 0.5, 0.16, 0.36, c=0.2); intersection_over_union returns about 0.34 for this pair. Compute this cell's contribution to box_loss (ignore epsilon).
questions.explanation: sqrt(0.25) = 0.5, sqrt(0.16) = 0.4, sqrt(0.36) is equal on both sides; placement errors are x5 and the occupied-cell confidence error is x1.

questions.question: What does box_loss return for a batch of 16 images?
options: A single scalar
A tensor of shape (16,)
A tensor of shape (16, 6, 6)
A tensor of shape (16, 6, 6, 5)
questions.answer: A tensor of shape (16,)
questions.explanation: ops.sum over axes (1, 2, 3) removes the grid and channel axes, leaving one value per sample. Keras then reduces over the batch; the other shapes are intermediate tensors.

questions.question: What evidence does the book give that the model is undertrained after Listing 12.12, and what does it imply?
questions.answer: Validation loss is still falling after 4 epochs, so training more would likely keep improving the model before overfitting starts.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says so, and p.370 lists 'Train for more epochs' among the improvements.

questions.question: Why does the book skip metrics, and which metric does it suggest you'd want in practice?
questions.answer: Purely to keep the example short; in practice you'd want metrics such as model accuracy at different confidence cutoff levels.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph before Listing 12.12.

questions.question: Can you point to the exact line in Listing 12.11 that implements each of the three tricks from p.367?
questions.answer: x5: the two ops.where(no_object, 0.0, ... * 5.0) lines; x0.5: ops.where(no_object, conf_error * 0.5, conf_error); sqrt: wh_error = ops.square(signed_sqrt(wh_true) - signed_sqrt(wh_pred)).
questions.explanation: Linking prose to code is the key skill for reading custom losses.

questions.question: What does `val_dataset.rebatch(1)` do in Listing 12.13?
options: Shuffles the validation set
Re-splits the batches so each element holds a single sample
Repeats the dataset once
Removes the labels
questions.answer: Re-splits the batches so each element holds a single sample
questions.explanation: The callout says it rebatches to get a single sample instead of 16. It doesn't shuffle, repeat or drop labels (y is still returned).

questions.question: What is the shape of `classes` after the argmax, and what does each entry represent?
questions.answer: (6, 6); each entry is the index of the most likely of the 91 COCO labels for that grid cell.
questions.explanation: preds['class'][0] is (6, 6, 91) and argmax over axis -1 removes the last axis.

questions.question: Why is `metadata[0]['path']` the correct image for the prediction?
questions.answer: Because val_dataset is dataset.take(500), the first batches in metadata order, so its first sample after rebatching is metadata[0].
questions.explanation: Listing 12.9 built the dataset from metadata in order and split validation off the front.

questions.question: In figure 12.6 the box is labeled 'giraffe 0.16'. What is 0.16?
options: The class probability of 'giraffe'
The predicted confidence of that cell's box
The IoU with the true box measured on the validation set
The loss value
questions.answer: The predicted confidence of that cell's box
questions.explanation: draw_prediction prints the box's confidence channel. It was trained toward IoU but is the model's prediction, not a measured IoU; the class probability is not printed.

questions.question: Why does the book use a cutoff of only 0.1?
questions.answer: Because the undertrained model outputs low confidences; a higher cutoff would hide even correct boxes.
questions.explanation: p.368 announces a low-confidence cutoff because the model is not a very good detector yet.

questions.question: Without looking, can you explain what happens inside draw_prediction when cutoff=None?
questions.answer: `not cutoff` is True, so the condition passes for every cell and all 36 boxes are drawn.
questions.explanation: This is the mechanism behind figure 12.7.

questions.question: According to the book, why does the model learn very low confidence values?
options: The confidence output has a sigmoid that saturates
It has not yet learned to consistently locate objects in a scene
The class loss dominates the box loss
The cutoff in draw_prediction was too high
questions.answer: It has not yet learned to consistently locate objects in a scene
questions.explanation: This is the book's stated reason. The box output has no activation (p.362), the book doesn't claim the class loss dominates, and the cutoff only affects drawing, not learning.

questions.question: List the five improvements the authors suggest for the YOLO model.
questions.answer: Train for more epochs; use the whole COCO dataset; data augmentation (translating and rotating images and boxes); improve the class probability map for overlapping boxes; predict multiple boxes per grid location using a bigger output grid.
questions.explanation: These are the five bullets on the page.

questions.question: Why must data augmentation for object detection transform the boxes as well as the images?
questions.answer: Because the labels are spatial: if the image is shifted or rotated but the boxes are not, the targets no longer match the objects' positions.
questions.explanation: The bullet explicitly says 'translating and rotating input images and boxes'.

questions.question: Which limitation of the book's model does 'Predict multiple boxes per grid location' address?
options: Two objects centered in the same cell can't both be detected
The class loss is not differentiable
The images are too large for memory
The backbone is not pretrained
questions.answer: Two objects centered in the same cell can't both be detected
questions.explanation: With one box per cell, each cell detects at most one object. The class loss is differentiable, memory is handled by tf.data, and the backbone is pretrained.

questions.question: Why does the chapter switch to a pretrained RetinaNet rather than applying all the improvements?
questions.answer: Training an accurate COCO detector from scratch would take a large amount of compute and time; the YOLO example was only meant to give a feel for detection training.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph before section 12.3.

questions.question: What do RetinaNet and the book's YOLO model have in common?
questions.answer: Both are single-stage object detectors operating on the same basic principles: predicting boxes and labels in one pass.
questions.explanation: First sentence of section 12.3; p.356 lists both as single-stage families.

questions.question: Looking at figure 12.7, can you explain why most boxes are labeled 'unlabeled' and where the 'giraffe' boxes cluster?
questions.answer: Cells predicted as label 0 (no object) are named 'unlabeled'; the giraffe-labeled boxes cluster in the cells around the giraffe, matching the class map in figure 12.6.
questions.explanation: Connecting the class map to the drawn labels tests your understanding of draw_prediction.

questions.question: Why are the final ConvNet outputs not very effective at finding small objects?
options: They have too many channels
Their features map to large areas of the input image
They are not trained
They contain only edge detectors
questions.answer: Their features map to large areas of the input image
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page. Channel count is not the problem; they are trained (pretrained ResNet); edge-like features are characteristic of early layers, not final ones.

questions.question: Why not simply use the outputs of early layers to detect small objects?
questions.answer: They are high-resolution but not semantically interesting: they represent simple features like edges and curves, while object-level representations only form in later layers.
questions.explanation: The second printed paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Describe the two ingredients of a feature pyramid network according to the book and what each contributes.
questions.answer: Progressive upsampling of the final features with Conv2DTranspose layers (spreading semantic information to higher resolutions) and lateral connections that sum each upsampled map with the same-size backbone map (injecting high-resolution detail).
questions.explanation: Together they combine semantically rich low-resolution features with high-resolution small-scale features.

questions.question: In figure 12.8, what do the arrows leaving each map on the right-hand stack represent?
options: Gradients flowing back
Predictions made at each scale of the pyramid
Lateral connections
Downsampling steps
questions.answer: Predictions made at each scale of the pyramid
questions.explanation: Each top-down level is a usable feature map that feeds outputs; lateral connections are the horizontal arrows from left to right, and downsampling is the upward left-hand path. Gradients aren't drawn.

questions.question: Why does the lateral connection combine maps 'of the same size'?
questions.answer: Because the maps are summed element-wise, which requires matching spatial dimensions.
questions.explanation: The upsampling steps are designed to reach exactly the resolutions of the backbone stages.

questions.question: Why do the authors test RetinaNet on a pointillist painting?
questions.answer: It is out-of-distribution for a model trained on COCO photographs, so it tests whether the detector generalizes beyond the pixel statistics of its training data.
questions.explanation: The page calls it out-of-distribution 'to make this a little more interesting'; p.373 reports the result.

questions.question: Can you sketch figure 12.8 from memory and label the bottom-up path, top-down path, lateral connections and outputs?
questions.answer: Left: image with shrinking backbone maps (bottom-up). Right: maps growing downward (top-down). Horizontal arrows: lateral connections. Arrows out of the right stack: per-level predictions.
questions.explanation: If you can do this, you understand the FPN structure the page describes.

questions.question: What does the 'rel' in the bounding-box format "rel_xywh" mean?
options: Coordinates are relative to the box's centre
Coordinates are relative to the image size, in [0, 1]
Coordinates are relative to the previous detection
Coordinates are relative to the feature-map grid cell
questions.answer: Coordinates are relative to the image size, in [0, 1]
questions.explanation: The page states that rel stands for relative to the image size (e.g., from [0, 1]). Box-centre offsets and grid-cell-relative coordinates are other encodings (the YOLO targets on p.363 put x, y relative to the grid cell, but that is internal to the YOLO training setup), and nothing is relative to a previous detection.

questions.question: Why does Listing 12.15 loop over range(num_detections) instead of over all 100 boxes?
questions.answer: Because the outputs are padded to a fixed size of 100; only the first num_detections entries are valid detections.
questions.explanation: The page shows boxes with shape (1, 100, 4) and a separate num_detections output. A fixed maximum keeps tensor shapes rectangular; the count tells you how many slots are real.

questions.question: Why do the authors pass bounding_box_format="rel_xywh" rather than accepting the model's default?
questions.answer: So the boxes use the same format as the YOLO model and the chapter's box-drawing utilities can be reused without conversion.
questions.explanation: The page says exactly this; draw_box (p.358) unpacks x, y, w, h on a unit canvas, so relative xywh boxes plot correctly.

questions.question: What is the shape of `image` after `np.array([keras.utils.load_img(path)])`, and why the list brackets?
questions.answer: (1, height, width, 3); the list adds a batch axis of size 1 because Keras models predict on batches.
questions.explanation: load_img returns one RGB image; wrapping it in a list and converting gives a batch of one, consistent with the (1, ...) leading dimension of every output.

questions.question: Which component does the preset name 'retinanet_resnet50_fpn_v2_coco' NOT tell you?
options: The backbone architecture
The dataset the model was trained on
The bounding-box format of the output
That a feature pyramid network is used
questions.answer: The bounding-box format of the output
questions.explanation: resnet50 names the backbone, coco the training data, fpn the feature pyramid network. The box format is chosen separately via the bounding_box_format argument.

questions.question: A 1280×860 image contains a box whose top-left corner is at pixel (384, 172) and which is 256 px wide and 344 px tall. Write it in rel_xywh. Then check whether the printed box [0.53, 0.00, 0.81, 0.29] is a valid rel_xywh box.
questions.answer: (0.3, 0.2, 0.2, 0.4). The printed box would need x + w ≤ 1, but 0.53 + 0.81 = 1.34, so as xywh it would extend past the right edge.
questions.explanation: Divide x and w by 1280 and y and h by 860: 384/1280 = 0.3, 172/860 = 0.2, 256/1280 = 0.2, 344/860 = 0.4. For the printed box, the sum exceeds 1, which suggests those numbers are corner coordinates (x1, y1, x2, y2) rather than xywh — a point flagged for review.

questions.question: Can you list the four outputs of the detector and explain the role of each in drawing figure 12.9?
questions.answer: boxes give rectangles, labels give COCO class ids (converted to names and colours), confidence gives the score of each detection, num_detections gives how many slots to read.
questions.explanation: If you can connect each output to a line of Listing 12.15 (p.372–373), you understand the inference flow.

questions.question: According to the authors, why does RetinaNet generalize well to the pointillist painting?
options: It was fine-tuned on a dataset of paintings
Single-stage detectors draw on features from the entire input, and paintings share high-level structure with photos
Pointillist paintings look like photographs at the pixel level
It uses Selective Search to propose regions
questions.answer: Single-stage detectors draw on features from the entire input, and paintings share high-level structure with photos
questions.explanation: The page says paintings and photos differ at the pixel level (so option 3 is backwards) but share high-level structure. No painting training took place, and Selective Search belongs to early R-CNNs (p.355), not RetinaNet.

questions.question: What does `keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name(label)` do in the loop?
questions.answer: It converts the integer COCO class id predicted by the model into a human-readable name such as 'person' or 'dog'.
questions.explanation: Labels are integer ids; the utility (introduced on p.364) maps them to names used as the box text.

questions.question: Why is classifying small image patches in isolation 'extra difficult' for a painting?
questions.answer: A small patch of a pointillist painting is mostly dots of colour, which look very different from patches of training photographs; without the surrounding context, the classifier cannot rely on the shared high-level structure.
questions.explanation: The page contrasts pixel-level differences with high-level similarity; isolated patches expose only the former.

questions.question: Which object classes are visible in figure 12.9?
questions.answer: person, umbrella and dog.
questions.explanation: The figure shows multiple person boxes, two umbrella boxes and two dog boxes on the painting.

questions.question: Which line of Listing 12.15 is outside the for-loop?
options: box = predictions["boxes"][0][i]
label_name = keras_hub.utils.coco_id_to_name(label)
draw_box(ax, box, label_name, label_to_color(label))
plt.show()
questions.answer: plt.show()
questions.explanation: The first four lines are indented under `for i in range(num_detections):` (p.372); plt.show() is dedented and runs once after all boxes are drawn.

questions.question: Can you explain, in your own words, one advantage of single-stage detectors mentioned in this chapter other than robustness?
questions.answer: They are generally faster and more efficient, suitable for real-time applications.
questions.explanation: The chapter summary on p.374 states this; this page adds robustness to novel inputs.

questions.question: What is YOLO's box confidence score trained to predict for a grid cell that contains an object?
options: 1, always
The class probability of the object
The Intersection over Union of the predicted and ground-truth boxes
The area of the predicted box
questions.answer: The Intersection over Union of the predicted and ground-truth boxes
questions.explanation: The summary states this explicitly (and p.367 explains it). A constant 1 would ignore box quality; class probability is a separate output; box area is not a quality measure.

questions.question: A predicted box spans x 0–0.4, y 0–0.4; the true box spans x 0.2–0.6, y 0.2–0.6. What is the IoU, and thus YOLO's target confidence?
Why do the authors call object detection 'a weaker version of image segmentation'?
questions.answer: Because a bounding box conveys less information than a per-pixel mask: it localizes the object only coarsely. In return it is much more efficient to run.
questions.explanation: The first summary bullet makes both points.

questions.question: What problem does a feature pyramid network solve, and how?
questions.answer: Detecting objects of very different sizes. It combines features from multiple ConvNet layers into feature maps at different scales, so high-resolution maps carry deep semantic information too.
questions.explanation: The fourth bullet; p.371 details the upsampling plus lateral-connection mechanism.

questions.question: Which detector is two-stage?
options: YOLO
RetinaNet
R-CNN
All single-pass ConvNet detectors
questions.answer: R-CNN
questions.explanation: R-CNNs propose regions and then classify them; YOLO and RetinaNet are named as single-stage.

questions.question: Without looking, can you explain why single-stage detectors suit self-driving cars, and name one more advantage of them from p.373?
questions.answer: They are faster and more efficient (real-time); they also use whole-image features, making them more robust to novel inputs.
questions.explanation: Speed comes from the summary; robustness from p.373.
